utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom and outside listening to these procedures. At the outset of today's hearing, the Chamber would like to raise three matters. The first one is an explanation of the position of the Chamber in regards to the Prosecution's addendum of the 29th of June, 2010, to its 94 bis notice regarding Witness Kathryn Barr and the response of the Defence of 5th of August. The Trial Chamber wishes to explain its position on the Prosecution's addendum to its 94 bis notice of disclosure. The Trial Chamber will not be issuing a formal decision in relation to it. In the Prosecution's addendum, the Prosecution sought leave from the Trial Chamber to supplement its Rule 94 bis disclosure with the addition of an expert report by Kathryn Barr, the Witness 9. On the 5th of August, 2010, the Defence filed a response in which it requests that the Prosecution's addendum be denied and that if the Trial Chamber finds that the Prosecution's addendum should be granted, it gives notice that it wishes to cross-examine the expert witness concerned. In the 92 bis decision of 7th of July, the Trial Chamber decided to provisionally admit the evidence of Kathryn Barr, pursuant to Rule 92 bis subject to her appearing for cross-examination. Rule 94 bis gives the Trial Chamber the discretion to allow the admission into evidence of an expert report or a statement without calling the expert to testify in person, if the opposing party accepts it. Where, as here, the opposing party does not accept the expert report, the issue of admissibility pursuant to Rule 94 bis does not arise. The Trial Chamber therefore is not rendering a decision with regard to the additional expert report by Kathryn Barr disclosed in the Prosecution's addendum. This is without prejudice to any motions that the Prosecution might make in regard to it in the future. This was the first matter. Now the Chamber would like to issue an oral decision. The Chamber is presently seized of the remainder of the Prosecution's motion for leave to amend the witness list, admission of evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter and protective measures, which was filed confidentially on the 15th of July, 2010, and hereby renders its decision thereon. As it was the case for the other part of this decision which was rendered last week, this motion was prompted by the Prosecution's recent review of its intercept evidence, wherein it was noted that the conversations intercepted by this proposed witness are, in the view of the Prosecution, sufficiently proximate to the acts and conduct of the accused to warrant his appearance in court for the purposes of cross-examination. He recorded six intercepted conversations which were admitted through a different witness during the Popovic case and he was interviewed by telephone on the 30th of June, this year. On the 18th of August, 2010, the accused responded. This response was filed confidentially. The parties made oral submissions on the motion on Thursday of last week, the 19th of August, this year. For the sake of brevity, I will not reiterate the submissions of the parties here. The first question before the Chamber is whether it is in the interests of justice to add the witness to the Rule 65 ter witness list. The Chamber appreciates that the motion is aimed to give the accused the opportunity to challenge the evidence of this witness. Although the accused rightly points out that his evidence will largely focus on the authentication of the intercepts, it is precisely this authenticity that the accused has repeatedly challenged. The Chamber notes that the Prosecution proposes that the witness testify pursuant to Rule 92 ter and encloses a draft witness statement, which is only one page long and contains nine short paragraphs. As for the intercepts proposed for admission through this witness, the Chamber notes that they were included on the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter exhibit list, were proposed for admission and were provisionally admitted through another witness who was the subject of the Prosecution's Rule 92 bis motion. Under these circumstances, the Chamber considers that the accused would not be prejudiced by the witness's addition to the Rule 65 ter witness list at this stage of the proceedings. However, not surprisingly, as regards the timing of this witness's testimony, the Chamber reiterates its concern that the Prosecution's practice of scheduling a witness to appear before the Chamber has taken a particular decision which is a precondition for the witness to appear at all; and the Chamber would prefer that the Prosecution schedule the witness for later this week in order to permit the accused to have sufficient time to prepare for cross-examination. The Chamber trusts that this unfortunate scheduling situation will not occur again. The Chamber will now address the portion of the Prosecution's motion which relates to the admission of the witness's witness statement as well as the intercepts pursuant to Rule 92 ter. The accused submits that the draft statement in appendix C to the motion does not meet the requirements of admission pursuant to Rule 92 ter because it is a draft statement which does not bear the signature of the proposed witness. The Chamber notes that, unlike Rule 92 bis (B), Rule 92 ter does not set out requirements for the written statements and, as noted by the Prosecution, the witness will attest to his statement under oath. Accordingly, the accused does not provide a sufficient reason to deny the Prosecution's motion to admit the witness's statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter, provided that the witness appears in court and complies with the conditions set out in Rule 92 ter. In relation to the intercepts themselves, however, the Chamber notes that they are not mentioned in the witness statement and therefore cannot be admitted as exhibits associated with it. The Prosecution, of course, remains free to use these intercepts with the witness when he appears in court. For these reasons, the Prosecution's motion to admit the evidence of this witness is granted in relation to the witness statement, pending the fulfilment of the Rule 92 ter conditions upon this witness's appearance in court. However, the motion to admit the intercepts pursuant to Rule 92 ter is denied. Finally, the Chamber notes that on the 18th of August, 2010, the Prosecution filed a confidential motion seeking the protective measures of a pseudonym and facial distortion for this witness. The motion may not yet have been translated into B/C/S. Mr. Tolimir, are you aware of this motion?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Presiding Judge. I'd like to greet you and, yes, I am aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And do you intend to respond to this motion and are you prepared to do that orally today?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Tolimir's microphone be turned towards Mr. Tolimir, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my opinion and that of my attorney that the Chamber should decide on that because I believe you will also take our interests into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The interpreters asked you to move a little bit further to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber grants this motion, although it's not officially necessary to have a decision by the Chamber. The protective measures shall continue as in the previous trial. We have now another witness available for today, and there's a request for continuation of protective measures. I think in this case, again, it is not necessary to have an official and formal decision on the protective measures, as they continue like in the last trial according to your motion we have received this morning. The witness should be brought in. The screens are -- will be closed for this procedure, that the witness can enter the court and will be opened after that again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. First, thank you for your patience. We start a little bit later. We had some procedural matters to discuss. Would you now please read aloud the affirmation on the card to tell the truth which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is not the first time that you are giving evidence in this Tribunal. You know the procedure and you must know that the protective measures granted by another Chamber are still in place for you. Mr. Thayer for the Prosecution has, I suppose, some questions for you. Mr. Thayer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you and Your Honours. Good afternoon to the Defence. Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we may go into private session for just a couple of biographical details for some moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At some point, sir, did you move from your native village?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Sometime in early June there was a clash or the conflict broke out. My village, as well as a number of surrounding villages, were taken over by the Army of Republika Srpska and torched. Basically all of the residents, including myself, left the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where did you go, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: For a while we lived on a nearby mountain. It is Mount Brloska. Then we went to a settlement in the municipality of Srebrenica called Zeleni Jadar. We found some sort of accommodation there. I think it used to be a factory that had to do with wood processing. I spent most of my time there until my mother died, which was in late February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Why did you move all the way over to the area of Zeleni Jadar in the Srebrenica municipality, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Well, since we had no place to stay anymore and we did not have food, there was greater possibility to find food in Srebrenica at the time and one could also find accommodation. That was the reason why we went there. Most of the population did the same thing, the people of my and surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's for a moment go back a little bit 1992. Do you recall the VRS launching an attack from the area of Han Pijesak; and if you do, would you describe, please, for the Trial Chamber the directions of that attack and just briefly what happened during that attack?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, although it's been a while, the Army of Republika Srpska launched an attack from the direction of Han Pijesak, whereupon they took over the following villages, Krivace, Rijeka, Podzeplje, Brloznik, Stoborani, and Godjenje [Realtime transcript read in error "Stoponi, and Glodjane"], and perhaps a number of villages in the municipality of Rogatica, such as Klaze [as interpreted] and Vrtoce. This is where they established the new front line or a new line which was as far as we could go.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm looking at the transcript, sir, and I see one of the villages that -- actually, two of the villages you've identified as being Stoponi and Glodjane. Were those the correct names, sir, or are they known by other names?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: No. Stoborani and Godjenje as well as Laze instead of Klaze.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I think sometime in the future the Trial Chamber will have an opportunity to look at some maps, maybe with you, maybe with another witness. The -- your native village, sir, you testified was torched. I just want to call your attention to another village by the name of Borak. Can you describe what happened to that village?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: As far as I recall, that village remained intact until July 1995. The local residents lived there normally. After the take-over of Zepa in July 1995, I suppose the village was occupied. I don't know whether the houses were burned, though, because I did not see it. Borak, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the front line or confrontation line, as you described it, formed by these villages that you've named, was that confrontation line more or less in place in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes, although I cannot recall all of the details or micro-locations. Generally, however, the line remained as such from early 1992 to July 1995. I should also add that it was the southern side of the then-Zepa enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. You told us a few moments ago, sir, that you arrived in the Srebrenica area in 1993. Please tell the Trial Chamber what was going on.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: First I'd like to make a small correction. I think I arrived in Zeleni Jadar and Srebrenica in the fall of 1992, and I stayed there until the spring of 1993. My basic problem there, which was shared by most, was how to come up with food. In that period of time, i.e., in early 1993 and late 1992, I went to the town of Srebrenica on a number of occasions looking for food. At our place of accommodation in Zeleni Jadar there were many refugees who mainly hailed from the municipality of Han Pijesak. In any case, the situation was quite grave. We lacked the basic necessities, the living conditions were poor, there was no food, and life was truly hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So did you leave the Srebrenica area at some point, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: I left the area of Srebrenica after my mother died in early March or in the first half of March. I cannot recall exactly. I then began living in Zepa, in the village of Stitkov Dol, with a local who had not left his house. I stayed there until July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Zepa in early March or the first half of March 1993, can you tell the Trial Chamber what was going on there and what the conditions were like.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: I visited Zepa a few times during my stay in Zeleni Jadar already. The situation in Zepa wasn't much better than in Zeleni Jadar. There were more refugees there than there were locals. The basic problem in Zepa, too, was food at that time as well as medication and other necessities. Generally speaking, that was the context in Zepa in the spring of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were there any military activities during this period of time, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: During this period of time, during the winter, there were no significant military activities. Come spring, I think it was April, there was an operation or an action of the Army of Republika Srpska aimed at Zepa. Following that operation, Zepa was declared a safe area by virtue of UN resolution. It is then that military activities in the area of Zepa ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's spend a little bit of time, Witness, describing the geography and terrain of Zepa. Would you describe, please, for the Trial Chamber what people mean generally when they speak of the Zepa enclave. Is it a city? Is it a village? A group of villages?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: The enclave of Zepa is a small location in Eastern Bosnia. It is situated at the River Drina, at the Drina River basically. Zepa is somewhat larger than a simple village. When referred to as such, Zepa comprises a number of villages around the centre of Zepa. So the term "the Zepa enclave" includes a number of villages. Before the war, administratively Zepa had been a local commune of the Rogatica municipality. It wasn't a municipality as such. Geographically speaking, the centre of Zepa is at an altitude of some 5- to 600 metres above sea level. To the north of Zepa itself, there's a high mountain exceeding 1500 metres in height. On the northern side --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- at the southern side there's a plateau which is around 1.000 metres above sea level. Geographically speaking, Zepa is in a depression. As such, Zepa can be more easily defended in military terms as opposed to, say, some other locations which did not have such features around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how close, roughly speaking, is the enclave of Zepa from the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: The Srebrenica enclave is north of the Zepa enclave, and the distance between the centre of Zepa and the city of Srebrenica or the town of Srebrenica, rather, I would estimate -- of course I can't tell you precisely, but I would say that it is about 40 kilometres as the crow flies, 35, 40. And if we're talking about the entire enclave, for a while the two enclaves bordered on each other or actually relied on each other, and you could go from Zepa to Srebrenica on foot, not by car. And when I say that you could go from one enclave to the other, I have in mind the villages which bordered on the general area of the Zepa enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you arrived, sir, in 1993, what type of civilian authority existed there?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: As I've already stated, before the war Zepa was just a local commune and it belonged to Rogatica municipality. In principle, it did not have any organised institutions. When I finally arrived in Zepa, there was a War Presidency there. It existed in some shape or form and it tried as much as it could to control the situation. Although, in view of the overall developments, hunger and the rest, at that time the four or five people that constituted the War Presidency could not really have any influence on the organisation of life or the organisation of normal life at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what happened then, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Well, when Zepa was declared a protected area or a protected enclave, the situation changed completely. UNPROFOR entered Zepa and the troops belonged to the Ukrainian Battalion. Zepa started receiving humanitarian aid through the UNHCR from the logistical centre, and as far as I know, that logistical centre was in Belgrade. Military observers also arrived, as well as Medecins Sans Frontieres. I don't know whether the latter arrived before the Red Cross, that also arrived. And in some way the situation became more stable, as it were. There was also a reorganisation of civilian authorities, or rather, their numbers of staff was increased. An Executive Board was established, and that body was supposed to look after the civilian population, the organisation of schools, health care, and finally, they're also supposed to look after the distribution of humanitarian aid. I was proposed and finally selected as the president of the Executive Board. From early May 1993, as far as I can remember, until April 1995, I discharged the duties of the president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You told us a few moments ago that at the time of your arrival the War Presidency was not functioning, basically. Would you describe for the Trial Chamber whether the War Presidency was reconstituted or did become functioning; and if so, what was its relationship to the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Well, look, let me explain. The War Presidency - I apologise - was a body which had been set up pursuant to the laws which were still in effect, and those laws had been adopted from the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. War Presidencies consisted of the current mayor or the president of the municipality, the president of the Executive Board, and maybe I should say what the Executive Board is. It's an executive body which corresponds with the position of a prime minister in a state. Of course there's no real comparison, but that would be that. And then another member of the Executive Board is also the head of the civilian protection or whatever his title was, and also the highest-ranking military commander. And if my memory serves me well, that would be that. I don't know if there was anybody else. In other words, the establishment of the Executive Board at the time meant that all the necessary functions were completed to organise the civilian life in Zepa. In other words, that was one thing that was lacking because before that there was no municipal organisation as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in 1993 when the War Presidency was reconstituted or made more functional, was there an actual president of the War Presidency; and if so, who was it in 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Yes, there was a president. It was a long time ago, but I believe that three men occupied that position. But at that moment the first one that I remember was Mr. Benjamin Kulovac and he was the one who proposed that I should become the president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we'll hear more about Dr. Kulovac later, sir. In 1995, and specifically in July of 1995, who was the president of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: In July 1995 the president of the War Presidency of Zepa - I apologise - was Mr. Mehmed Hajric.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Hajric's occupation?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Mehmed Hajric was a religious official. He was a hodza. If you will allow me to use the jargon. That was the title of his function or the position for which he had been educated and which he discharged at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I'll ask you some more specific questions about Mr. Hajric and his role in the community later, sir. But just very briefly, if you could describe what a hodza is. You've described him so far as a religious official, but what are the duties or functions of a hodza?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Well, in the organisation of an Islamic community, the main person or the number one person in a mosque that covers a certain area and a certain number of followers is a hodza. He is the one who is performing religious services in that mosque and he has an area to cover and a certain number of people to administer to. And as in all other religions, a hodza is a man whom people respect and trust, at least those people who believe in God, who are church-going or mosque-going people.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in July of 1995, what were the duties of the war president -- or I should say the president of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: The president of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Well, the president of the War Presidency by virtue of his duties and function maintained contacts with the representatives of UNPROFOR and other international organisations. He also discharged all the other duties that the position entailed. Perhaps I was not clear enough, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think we can keep moving, sir. Thank you. The Trial Chamber may hear reference from witnesses to the mayor of Zepa. And in 1995 if somebody referred to the mayor of Zepa, who would that have been?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Well, that would have been the president of the War Presidency. The mayor equalled that position because the mayor was also the president of the War Presidency, and in this specific case during that period of time that was Mr. Mehmed Hajric. He was the number one person in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if there's a reference in the testimony to a deputy mayor, who would that have been in July of 1995, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: The deputy of a mayor was the president of the Executive Board, and that would be me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now that you've generally described some of the tasks of the War Presidency and Executive Board as including the distribution of aid and the establishment of a school, can you give the Trial Chamber just a little bit more detail on the real nuts and bolts of what the War Presidency and its Executive Board was fundamentally responsible for in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: The main duties and functions of the Executive Board as a basic organisational unit of civilian authorities in Zepa were to organise education and relaunch education in the centre of Zepa as well as into regional schools that had stopped working for a year due to war activities. Secondly, to the largest extent possible, to organise the system of health care, and that could not have been done without help from outside, without medicines delivered by the Red Cross and the organisation of Medecins Sans Frontieres. Last, but certainly not least, was to organise distribution of humanitarian aid and that aid arrived in Zepa from the logistics centre of the UNHCR in Belgrade. I've already emphasised that. There was also something else. As developments ensued, since about 60 per cent of the total population of Zepa which resided there at the time consisted of refugees or displaced persons, in other words, those people who had arrived from the municipalities of Han Pijesak, Visegrad, Rogatica, and from some other municipalities such as Vlasenica, but their numbers were smaller. It was necessary to try and organise additional accommodation capacities for them. That's why with the assistance of the UNHCR we launched an operation. The UNHCR delivered the necessary material and people built little houses where they could accommodate their families. Those were the basic activities of the Executive Board. Within the War Presidency, there also existed the civilian protection as one of its organisational units. In certain matters the civilian protection was supposed to lend a hand to the population. They were particularly engaged in the construction of those small residential dwellings. Within the framework of the War Presidency as an independent organisational unit, there was also the civilian police. Its chief was also a member of the War Presidency by virtue of his position. Another member of the War Presidency was also the main military commander in Zepa. In organisational terms, those were people who constituted the War Presidency. The War Presidency composition covered all the organisations that existed in Zepa at the time. So much about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's put some names to some positions. Who was the head of civilian protection, sir, and I should add in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: The head of the civilian protection and a member of the War Presidency was Mr. Amir Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we'll certainly hear more about Mr. Imamovic later today. Did the civilian protection organisation have any police or military duties, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: No, they were not incorporated into that part of the organisation, either the police or the military organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you, in fact, did refer to the civilian police. Who headed that organisation, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: The civilian police was headed by Mr. Hurem Sahic throughout the entire war, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You also referred to the main military commander being a member of the War Presidency. Who was that in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: That was Avdo Palic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The name of the organisation being the War Presidency and having a member of the board or of the War Presidency being the top military commander in the area, did the War Presidency or the Executive Board have any military functions, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: The War Presidency was supposed to decide on all matters concerning life in the enclave. Most probably there was a problem that existed. When the military became active, as it were, the brigade was part of the military system and they had their own lines of command. It may have happened that the interests of a local population did not tally completely or did not agree with some of the military actions that were undertaken at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So was Mr. Palic and his military chain of command independent or part of the Executive Board and War Presidency? And you've already told us Mr. Palic sat on it, but was there a regular -- any type of regular communication or consultation or involvement of yourself, the Executive Board, with Mr. Palic's military decision-making, for example?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: There were lines of communication. The most important things were also presented to the War Presidency. However, some of the key things and the commands to the military organisation is something that the commander, Palic, received along the lines of his own command, not from the War Presidency in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how informed were you - "you" meaning the Executive Board - of Colonel Palic's day-to-day military activities and decision-making?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: No, not on day-to-day military activities, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions before we take the first break, and then I'll move to a new area, sir. When you arrived in Zepa in 1993, approximately how many people, to the best of your recollection, lived in the area that you've been talking about as comprising Zepa?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: When the first convoy of humanitarian aid arrived, we had to try and establish the approximate number of people who resided in the area. As far as I can remember, that number was slightly over 7.000 people in the entire territory of the Zepa enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And by July of 1995, did that number go up or did it go down?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: It is possible that between the initial period and July 1995 there were population migrations, and that number probably fluctuated and increased at times. However, in July 1995, as far as I can remember, there were approximately 7.000 people living in Zepa. I would like to emphasise that that situation changed depending on the food situation. There were times that during that period of two years that number did go up and surpassed the initial 7.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just explain for us, please, what the relationship is or was between the food situation and the numbers in Zepa going up.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Could you please be more precise. You're asking me about the food situation and the increase of the population numbers in Zepa? Is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Exactly, sir. You testified that: "... the situation changed depending on the food situation. There were times that during that period of two years that number did go up and surpassed the initial 7.000." Why would the number be increased depending on the food situation?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Now I understand your question. The Srebrenica enclave was next to Zepa and Srebrenica had a much larger population number. And what happened? I suppose that the humanitarian aid that arrived in Srebrenica did not meet the basic needs of the population there, and that's why the refugees who found accommodation in Srebrenica came to Zepa where the food situation was better. What did it mean? It meant that every week that they received a few more kilogrammes of flour more than if they had stayed in Srebrenica, and that is the main reason why the number of 7.000 people fluctuated, or rather, why it went up during one particular period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You told us a little while ago that approximately 60 per cent of the population in Zepa was comprised of refugees or displaced persons. Please tell the Trial Chamber why those people went to Zepa. What was the cause of them becoming displaced or refugees?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: In order to understand why they came to Zepa or in order to make everybody understand that, I had described the geographic position of Zepa. At the beginning of 1992 war in Bosnia started, and as I've already stated, there were municipalities in which residents had been forced to leave their places of residence and they were looking to physically move to a territory where they would feel safer. In other words, Han Pijesak, where I was living, had a number of villages inhabited by Muslims. A line was established at the very beginning. The VRS occupied those villages, and the only place where the population could go was towards Zepa. In geographical terms that was the only place where they could find shelter, the only place where they could go. And the same applied to the municipalities of Visegrad, Rogatica, where combat had taken place and the population from those municipalities and villages ended up in Zepa as refugees or displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, before you continue, we would like to clarify one term. Is the War Presidency the same body as the Executive Board or are these different bodies?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you field that question for His Honour, sir, please?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Of course. The Executive Board or an Executive Board is a special organisational body which looks after different aspects of civilian life in an area. Its number one person, according to the then-prevalent laws, was a member of the War Presidency. In other words, one can say that the Executive Board is one of the organisational units or one part of the War Presidency. Maybe that is the best answer. In addition to the Executive Board, there's also an independent civilian police, there's also an independent civilian protection, there's also military with its proper organisational units, and all the number one men of those bodies constitute another body known as a War Presidency. I hope that I've been of assistance and that I've clarified the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly that the Executive Board is one part of the -- or under the supervision of the War Presidency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Another question by Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. At the relevant time you were the president of the Zepa Executive Board; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Who was then the president of the Presidency at that same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During that same time, there were three presidents of the Presidency. And throughout all that time, I was the only president of the Executive Board. In other words, when the Executive Board was set up, or rather, when the War Presidency was constituted properly, the first president of the War Presidency was Benjamin Kulovac, as I've already stated. And he stayed in that position for a year, so I can't remember exactly. The next one who succeeded him was Mr. Ago Podzic, I believe. And the third president of the War Presidency was Mr. Mehmed Hajric. During those two years they changed, whereas I remained as the president of the Executive Board all that time. I hope my answer was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: It's clear, but I just need some further clarification. At page 20, line 14 to 17, of today's transcript, you state that: "... some of the key things and the commands to the military organisation is something that the commander, Palic, received along the lines of his own command, not from the War Presidency ..." From whom then did Palic receive his commands? In other words, who was his commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here's how it was. During the relevant time, in 1995, the BiH army was organised - and I'm only talking about the Zepa area, that's what I'm talking about - it was organised in the following way. In Srebrenica there was the 28th Division as an organisational unit of the 2nd Corps, I believe, but I'm not sure, and I believe it was based in Tuzla. Maybe somebody can help me with that. And in Zepa there was the 1st Light or 285th Zepa Brigade on the strength of the 28th Division, and the commander of that brigade in Zepa was Mr. -- Colonel, actually, Avdo Palic. And along the military line of command, he was part of the line that started with the corps and ended with the corps. He did sit on the War Presidency, but his orders arrived along his chain of command. I hope that I've been able to clarify the matter. When I interpreted the situation the first time, I may have confused all of you who have not previously come across this case and this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, some minutes left before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I may follow-up on Honourable Judge Nyambe's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So do you know who in July of 1995 was Colonel Palic's immediate superior officer? To whom within that military chain of command? You've described the 2nd Corps being based in Tuzla, the 28th Division being based in Srebrenica, and Mr. Palic's Zepa Brigade being subordinated to the 28th Division. Can you tell us, if you know, to whom did Mr. Palic directly report as his immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: I'm not a military expert; however, my logic tells me that he was supposed to be subordinated to the commander of the 28th Division. Although, however, I believe that he had a lot of direct contacts with the General Staff of the BiH Army, which means in other words that he was directly subordinated to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in July of 1995, do you know the name of the commander of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. The commander of that division, as far as I know, was Naser Oric. Sometime before he left the area of Srebrenica. I don't know whether he was replaced or whether that duty was discharged by the Chief of Staff. I really can't tell you because I don't know. I don't know whether anybody was appointed after Naser Oric or whether the Chief of Staff continued discharging those duties. I really can't tell you. I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I see we're at the break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We must have the first break now. The Court Officer will assist you during the break, but please be seated on safety reasons, please stay there. We adjourn quarter past 4.00 -- resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, sir.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You were telling us about the refugees and displaced people from the various municipalities who wound up living in Zepa. Describe, please, for the Trial Chamber, during this period of 1992 and 1993 when they went to Zepa from these other municipalities, what were the circumstances of their departure? What was happening to their homes and their mosques? Can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, about that.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: I'll do my best and I'll share at least the things I'm familiar with. I will go back to 1992 now, when Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised as a separate state. As far as I recall, it was the 5th or 6th of April, 1992. At that time the conflict broke out in Bosnia. As is well known, the Serb side rejected that outcome, and on the eve of Bosnia's recognition they undertook certain organisational measures. After Bosnia was recognised, in certain specific parts of Eastern Bosnia where I was, clashes erupted. I know precisely how it developed in the municipality of Pijesak, Han Pijesak, since I hail from there. All village residents within the municipality of Han Pijesak - and I mean Muslim villages - worked in two different wood processing plants in Han Pijesak. One was a sawmill and another was a furniture plant. In early May, around the 10th of May, when I attempted to go to work or when people attempted to go to work, two buses, if I'm not mistaken, carrying Muslim workers were stopped at a check-point just before entering Han Pijesak. All of them were returned to their villages. They were told to go back on foot. All road communication was cut off between those villages inhabited by Muslims and the municipal centre, i.e., Han Pijesak. One could no longer go to Han Pijesak. I think there were only a few instances on -- when ill people were let to pass through. The first military-type clash occurred in early June, on the 4th of June, if I remember correctly, when a column of what I still -- believe still at the time was the JNA attempted to reach a certain location called Zlovrh over Zepa. There was a clash with the Muslim side. By that time there was a certain degree of military organisation in existence on the side of the Bosnian army. Following that, there was a lull, and in late August and early September the army - which I don't know whether by that time was the Army of Republika Srpska - undertook a larger operation. Once the operation began, this offensive, people fled as would one expect. In this case they went to the mountainous terrain in the rear of those villages. All of the houses were torched, including entire villages. And the new lines that were established following that were located in such a way that people could no longer return to their villages. That population was left without anything, including food, medicine, et cetera. They lived literally in the forest. In my area I believe there were some 2.000 people in that situation. It was in the summer of 1992. During the fall, cold began setting in and people had to find accommodation to spend the winter. I presume similar happened in other municipalities, although I am not at liberty to discuss that since I was not there and I don't know how things developed. It is a fact, though, that a lot of people from other Muslim villages of the municipality of Rogatica as well as the Muslim villages in the Visegrad municipality ended up in Zepa in much the same way. This would be a short description of the background and of the things I went through in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe would like to put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, I just need a clarification. From -- on page 27, from line 16 to about line 22, you described a situation in a village, Han Pijesak, and you describe how two buses carrying Muslim workers were stopped at the check-point just before that village. I -- the situation you described here of just Muslims being in these buses, implying that in this village only Muslim lived there, was this a typical situation in Bosnia before the breakout of the war, that people -- that Muslims all lived in these villages and there were no other ethnic groups in these villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to explain. Han Pijesak is a town which is the centre or the seat of that municipality. Within the municipality, as in any other municipality, there are other settlements covering the whole territory of the municipality. In this instance those settlements were villages. In this part of the country towards Zepa, which is on the eastern side of the Han Pijesak municipality, there was a rather clear ethnic line dividing Serb and Muslim villages. Since your question is aimed at that, I can tell you that both ethnicities, of course, worked in those factories. As for the buses which drove the Muslims to work functioned in such a way because of the geographical characteristics. It just so happened that in a particular area there were all Muslims. However, this was not typical of Bosnia pre-1992. To a large extent there were mixed villages as well as larger settlements and cities. However, this was the case in our area. We would look into the geographical layout and perhaps after that you would get a better picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you described the homes being torched by the Serb forces, the Muslim homes being torched. Do you know what happened to the mosques in these various municipalities after the Muslims were forced to leave?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: As far as I know and as far as I could see in the village neighbouring mine, was that the mosques, depending on the way they were constructed, were either brought down or torched. In this specific case I think that mosque was destroyed by explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you were there at the time, sir. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what your understanding of the purpose of this campaign by Serb forces, which torched the Muslim homes and destroyed their mosques, was?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, at first I couldn't understand why it was being done. Later on I realised that this meant putting preconditions in place so that people could not return to the area; in other words, to cleanse the area of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You've told us already about the Ukrainian peacekeepers arriving in Zepa after it was declared a safe area. Just share with the Trial Chamber where they were based in Zepa and where they were deployed and approximately how many of them were there. My apologies for the compound question, but it might be a little quicker that way.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: I will try to follow the order in your question. After UNPROFOR entered Zepa and following the demilitarisation of Zepa which has not been mentioned so far, UNPROFOR set up its headquarters in the centre of Zepa in the elementary school. UNPROFOR was organised along the following lines: All entry points into the enclave had their respective check-points manned by UNPROFOR soldiers. I think at the outset there were about ten such check-points. I don't know whether the figure varied in different periods of time, but at each of those check-points, as far as I remember, there was an armoured personnel carrier as well as a group of soldiers. As I said, the headquarters was in the centre of Zepa in the elementary school. In such a way, UNPROFOR could control all exit and entry in Zepa. Basically only UNPROFOR was to -- was allowed to exit or enter Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And approximately how many peacekeepers were there and who was their commander on the ground there, in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Initially I think - and I heard this information along the way - there were some 120 Ukrainian Battalion UNPROFOR soldiers. Their commander was Mr. Sejmon Dudnjik, a colonel, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And by July of 1995, did that number of 120 Ukrainian peacekeepers -- was that number increased or decreased, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: No, I think it decreased. I don't know for certain, though. Only UNPROFOR knew that precisely. Towards the end, given all the events which took place, it seems to me that their numbers were far less than 120.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You referred to demilitarisation a few moments ago, so let's talk about that a little bit. When you use that term, just tell the Trial Chamber, please, what are you talking about, especially in the context of the creation of the safe areas in spring of 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: In 1993 through one of UN's resolution, among other areas, Zepa was declared a safe area too. As far as I remember, it also included an additional or local agreement signed by, I believe, General Mladic and the then B&H army commander Sefer Halilovic at Sarajevo airport in the presence of UNPROFOR. It was arranged that the Bosnian side was to hand-over all of its weapons, and I mean the fighters in Zepa, to UNPROFOR. The weapons were to be kept by UNPROFOR. I believe the Bosnian side -- the Serb side undertook to withdraw all heavy weaponry surrounding Zepa. Once UNPROFOR arrived, the demilitarisation process took place, otherwise there weren't all that many weapons. It was done in early May or mid-May 1993. Following that, the military organisation or structure ceased to exist in Zepa, nominally speaking. All protection functions were taken over by UNPROFOR from that moment on. That is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you -- I see you were careful to use the term "nominally speaking." Did Colonel Palic continue in his position and role as commander of the Zepa Brigade following the signing of the demilitarisation agreement?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Well, I can share what I remember with you. The first year between May 1993 and onwards, UNPROFOR prohibited any carrying of weapons. It was not tolerated for anyone in Zepa. Organisationally speaking, there was no mention of any army. The real situation was as follows: All military activities ceased, people no longer went to the lines in the sense of any defensive lines, and there were no people standing guard there. After May 1993, such a thing no longer existed in Zepa. Nominally speaking, the commander remained in his position. Some strengthening of positions occurred in mid-1994. The year before that was the year when there was no activity in that field. The army was not officially organised, they did not go to the lines, and that is what I can recall from that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So do you recall the period when things changed? You just referred to a strengthening of positions in mid-1994. Do you recall a period during which there was more than nominal constitution and involvement activities by the Bosnian Muslim army in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: I believe I meant to say in the second half of 1994. In any case, as far as I remember, there were no new organisational attempts that year either, but what I can recall is that from Sarajevo from the General Staff of the then-Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina some activities were initiated - and I'm careful to use diplomatic terms. This included forwarding weapons to Zepa. Certain preparations seem to have been undertaken for new potential clashes in Zepa and its environs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There's no need to be diplomatic right now anyway, sir. Please --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- tell the Trial Chamber in more detail what you're talking about when you say that weapons were forwarded to Zepa and certain preparations were made, to the extent that you were aware of them at the time. What was happening?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: At the time, as far as I know, on several occasions some weapons and ammunition was brought in by helicopters and perhaps such shipments also included other things the army in Zepa may have needed. I know that it was in the second part of 1994 and the first half of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in your official role as a member of the War Presidency and president of the Executive Board, were you notified or made aware ahead of time that these helicopter deliveries of weapons, ammunition, and materiel would be made or did you learn about it in some other way?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: In some other way. Officially I knew nothing about that beforehand. Such information was not supposed to be passed on to me and I wasn't aware of it before it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And why wasn't it supposed to be passed on to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: I tried to explain that at the beginning. It was within the system of army command of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Under the organisation as it existed at the time, such information only went as far as the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just tell us, please, how did you become aware of these helicopter deliveries?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Well, those helicopter deliveries happened by night mostly. It didn't take the Serbian side long to notice the helicopter fly-overs and they opened fire at the helicopters, so every citizen in Zepa could assume what that was all about. There were several such fly-overs, and that's also I knew when and how a helicopter arrived carrying something. Let me say once again that the helicopters didn't always bring weapons. They were also used to transport officers to Kakanj, Tuzla, and Sarajevo, and back. In such cases, no weapons were brought. Those flights did not have anything whatsoever to do with the military supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at any time prior to July 1995, sir, did you become aware of any specific military operations which were undertaken by the Armija, the Muslim forces, operating out of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: A slight correction. We were the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We were not the Muslim forces. And the answer is: Yes, I can confirm that there was an action or an operation which was undertaken. I believe that that was in June 1995. I believe that the operation took place - let me just try and locate that operation in geographical term - I believe it was in the north-west of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe and I, we both have an additional question. Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I just need some clarification. At page 34, lines 21 into page 35 to line 4, you are talking about those helicopter deliveries happened by night. Whose helicopters were these and who delivered them to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were helicopters of the BiH Army, of the then-BiH Army. And those deliveries of weapons and everything else were undertaken by the BiH Army, or the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to supply its units in Zepa and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And myself, I would like to take you back to page 35, line 8. It is stated here: "We were the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Have you at this relevant time been a member of the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was a member of civilian authorities, and when I said "we" I meant the entire enclave of Zepa, because the enclave of Zepa belonged to those parts which were under the control of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That would be that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me just, again, follow-up on one of Honourable Judge Nyambe's questions. The night-time flights that occurred and that drew the Serb fire, did you ever yourself observe such an incident, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: I believe so, at least once.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, were any of these helicopters brought down by Serb fire?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Yes. In early May 1995 one helicopter was brought down. It had probably been hit when fire was opened on it. It almost reached its landing place and that's where it crashed. At that time the helicopter did not carry any weapons but, unfortunately, officers on their way back from Kakanj. And as far as I know, of the 22 passengers, 11 or 12 of them were killed as well as a medical team on its way from Tuzla to Srebrenica. After that event, the flight operations were discontinued and after that there were no other helicopter flights on the part of the Army of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You were speaking about a particular military operation conducted by the ABiH forces operating out of Zepa, you said, to the north-west of the enclave. Do you recall any of the details about that operation?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Well, I can't provide you with many details because it was a different line of command, but I know that the order for that attack had come -- or it would have been logical for it to have come from the command of the 28th Division, i.e., from Srebrenica. And they themselves were supposed to receive that order from the 2nd Corps in Tuzla. The explanation was that help was to be brought to the Sarajevo theatre of war to bring relief to the troops there, and the operation was carried out. As far as I know, it did not have any significance from the military point of view but it could provide and it probably did provide the Serbian side with an alibi or with an excuse for the future attacks on the enclaves. In this specific case the enclave was Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, we understand that you're not a military officer, but based on your understanding at the time, what was the purpose of attacking a location to the north-west of the Zepa enclave in terms of helping out the Sarajevo theatre? How were the two related, if you understood that at the time, sir? Or if you didn't I can move on.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Can we please move on. I'd rather talk about something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you a couple of related questions not about the objective of the operation. Were you told about it beforehand?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Yes. As I think back, I can tell you that we were told about that operation beforehand. As far as I can remember, that operation was preceded by a meeting of the War Presidency. We discussed that order, and it was Commander Avdo Palic who told us that he had received that order and that it had to be implemented. As far as I can remember, most of the War Presidency members were against that operation, myself included. But Avdo said that he had received the order and that he would carry it out because that operation in any case was counter-productive in terms of the overall situation of our overall situation and the situation that we were in. That operation had more bad sides there than good sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in July of 1995, sir, can you estimate how many approximately able-bodied men there were in the Zepa enclave?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: According to my estimate, about 1200 able-bodied men. Let me just say that they were not all combatants and could not be considered combatants. As future developments showed, there were not enough weapons for all of them but also when you're talking about able-bodied men, you imply men between the ages of 18 and 60 and there were about 1200 such men.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this ties in to a question from the Honourable Presiding Judge. You told us that you were not a member of the army. During the war did you ever carry a gun, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: No, I never carried any weapons. At the beginning of the war, sometime in 1992, Avdo Palic, the then-commander, provided us with some communication means; and later on I learned that he had formally appointed me the chief of communications. That was a position in the military organisation. However, after the VRS offensive those communication means remained in the houses where the troops were billeted. Therefore, no communication means existed in Zepa as such up to the second half of 1994. Later on, I saw those reports drafted by Colonel Palic in 1994. When I provided my first testimony, I saw that I had been appointed as chief of communications. But let me tell you once again, I never carried arms and I never served in the army, in the former JNA, due to health problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's clarify just a couple of things that I see in the transcript, sir. The first was you referred to a VRS offensive and the communications means that you were talking about. Can you just tell us what you were referring to, such that there were no communications means existing in Zepa up to the second half of 1994. What were the communication means? How long did the ABiH have them and how did they become no longer available to the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, in 1992 a military operation was carried out. One of the detachments of the BH army launched an attack on a location in the vicinity of Zepa, and that location was controlled by the then-JNA -- or I don't know whether the military was still the JNA or something else. And in any case, they captured some hand-held radio sets which are normally used for communication between the troops of an army. When I said that, that's the communication means that I had in mind. I believe that those were RUP radios, it's the so-called Rupovka sets which were used by the former JNA as the communication means. After the VRS offensive, those went missing; in other words, they were no longer available. I suppose that they had stayed behind in Krivace village where Commander Avdo Palic had them stored. Until the second half of 1994, the army did not have any communication means, and then a group of people went to Kakanj on foot. I believe that they went to Kakanj and brought back new communication means, primarily the packet communications means. It's a protected radio communication line which was later used to communicate both at Srebrenica and Kakanj. I believe that several hand-held radio sets were brought back on that occasion, and that's what I had in mind when I provided my previous answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And focusing on that first group of RUP radios that the ABiH had for that limited period of time, what did Colonel Palic ask you to do with respect to those?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether I actually ever saw all of them. Rumours had it that they had to be made usable. I am an electrical engineer and I suppose that Colonel Palic thought that I might be of some assistance there. As far as I can remember, I never actually saw them. I just discussed them on one occasion with him, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you referred in one of your prior answers to later on seeing reports drafted by Colonel Palic. Can you just tell us what you're referring to there when you said a few moments ago, and I quote: "Later on I saw those reports drafted by Colonel Palic." What are you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: I'm talking about the following thing. During the relevant period or maybe five or six months after that, I did not have any communication with Colonel Palic. I spent most of the time in Zeleni Jadar searching for food mostly. There was no organisation in place to speak of. There was no base location or any such thing, and when I said that I saw things later or subsequently, I saw that report three or three and a half years ago. I had not seen it before. I had not been informed about it. The report was written in 1994, and in that report Colonel Palic had provided a history of the Zepa brigade, the names of the people who discharged certain duties during certain periods of time. And one of the positions that he mentions is my position as the chief of communications. That's what I meant when I said that I saw things thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So during the relevant time-period, were you aware, sir, that Colonel Palic had appointed you chief of communications?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: When I think back, I believe that I knew that. I can't deny the fact, but let me just say that for almost six months, there was almost no communication between me and him and I didn't take that whole thing seriously. And already in 1993, either in April or early May, I became the president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during your entire period of service on the Executive Board, did you ever provide any further service or consultations of any kind with respect to communications for the army?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Well, look, Palic and I are friends. We went to the same elementary school. We are the same generation. We saw each other almost every day. We at least said hello to each other every day. However, in terms of other activities, primarily military activities, I didn't have any. I didn't have any activities related to new communications means. A new person was appointed as chief of communications, and he's the one who had gone to bring back the radios. And while he was in Kakanj, he was trained to use the equipment. So there was no need at all for assistance to be provided locally.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you know that person's name?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: I believe that his family name is Gusic and I'm afraid I can't remember his first name. Gusic is his family name.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In your testimony just back up a page on page 41, you referred to your first testimony in 1994. Was 1994 the year of your first testimony, sir, or did you first testify during another year?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: No. I would like to see that page. I believe that I just said in my previous testimony. I didn't mention any years. I didn't testify in 1994, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you just tell the Trial Chamber approximately when you first testified in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Here? You mean here?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: That was three or three and a half years ago, in 2007, late March/early April.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now from the spring of 1993 when you arrived in Zepa, I think you told us you arrived in March, but from, say, the spring of 1993 until the spring of 1995, how would you describe the level of VRS activity in the Zepa area?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: During that period, as far as I can remember, there was occasional shelling but there were no infantry attacks against the Zepa enclave. I believe that the shelling in question always came in response to some of the events outside of the Zepa enclave, and I'm speaking from memory. In other words, there were no attacks, no infantry attacks. Every now and then from time to time there was shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say that you believed that this shelling came in response to events outside the Zepa enclave, what do you mean, sir, and what was struck by the shelling? What were the targets of the shelling on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: I said I had -- it had to do with certain events outside the Zepa enclave, I meant to say that they were probably retaliating for something.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again, what were the targets? What was struck by this retaliatory shelling?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: In Zepa itself for the most part there were no military targets. There were villages in the area. During that period of time there was no intensive shelling; however, in the period before that, they mainly targeted settlements, houses, Zepa itself and the houses in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now turning your attention to 1995, prior to the VRS attack in July, do you recall any particular shelling that occurred?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: I think I recall the shelling of the village of Pripecak. Shells came from the other side of the Drina. It is not Serbia. I think there were positions of the Visegrad Brigade there, of the Army of Republika Srpska. If asked to define the period, I'd say the latter part of June. It was a very extensive and intensive shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, prior to the VRS attack in July of 1995, do you recall any shelling that you perceived to be tied - to use your phrase - to events outside of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Yes. I think once they targeted the centre of Zepa. Speaking from memory, I believe it was the response of the VRS to NATO bombardment of certain targets at Jahorina. I think I can tie these two things together.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you give us a month, please, that shelling occurred?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: It's possible that it was in May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to turn to the events of July 1995 now, and I just wanted to double-check, see if there are any questions from the Trial Chamber on all the events that we've been talking to -- here to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your expectation was correct. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, I just need a clarification from the witness. I can't point out exactly the page of the transcript, but somewhere in your testimony you've said that you were appointed chief of communications by Palic, correct, at some point for six months -- something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll answer this way: The appointment came from Palic. I tried to clarify. That appointment, nominally speaking, was valid for a period of six months, although during that time I basically had no contact with Palic. Perhaps this explains it to a certain extent. Palic appointed me and it was in place for about six months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: For what period was this? Which six months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, it was in September 1992 until March 1993 more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. -- another question by Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness, I have a question. I was planning to put this to you when you talked about this at length, but I'm going to do it now before the break. If you look at the transcript page 30, line 10 to 12, page 30, line 10 to 12, I'll repeat, you talked about the destruction of your village and the surrounding villages. And you also pointed out that mosques were burned down or destroyed. And those which were destroyed, or rather, what you are sure of is that those buildings were destroyed by explosive devices. So I have two questions to put to you. The first one is the following. I would like to know whether you personally saw those mosques being burned down or destroyed in the surrounding villages or have you heard of this happening? That was my first question. As for the second question: As for the mosques that were destroyed by explosive devices, I would like to know, given that you said you had no military knowledge and given that there were military operations that were underway, I would like to know whether those explosive -- I'm going to rephrase this. I would like to know whether those mosques were destroyed during the course of military operations or whether explosive devices were set willingly to destroy those mosques but that was not part of military operations? So that's my second question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to go back to the first part of your question. I'm just looking for it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The question was if you eye-witnessed such a destruction of the mosques.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was the first part. I didn't see it personally. I didn't see the destruction itself, but I could see such locations a few days following that. Specifically I have in mind the mosque in the village I was born in. That was the first part. The second, perhaps you could assist me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second question is mosques that were destroyed by explosive devices. I wanted to know whether they had been set willingly but whether it was part of military operations or whether it wasn't part of military operations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe at the beginning when I discussed the cases I am aware of, I explained it somewhat. I am aware of other incidents from the press. There may have been cases when such things occurred during military operations or clashes, but most of the cases were of the other kind, that is to say, that the mosques were destroyed following the take-overs of locations, places. I believe that should be the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, would it be convenient for everybody to have the second break now before you turn to the next set of questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then we will adjourn now and resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, sir.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall the date Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: I do. The 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Following the fall of Srebrenica, were there any contacts between the VRS and the Zepa authorities?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Following the fall of Srebrenica on the 12th of July, 1995, on the same day, the War Presidency of Zepa through UNPROFOR, through Colonel Sejmon Dudnjik, the commander, received a call or a request to conduct talks with the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who or what party originated this call to conduct talks with the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Perhaps I should clarify. The War Presidency received that request through UNPROFOR. Colonel Sejmon Dudnjik, as far as I recall, forwarded that call to Colonel Palic, saying that he or somebody else who would be chosen to do so had to meet with representatives on the Serb side. Perhaps I can carry on in explaining the sequence of events. That request arrived later on the 12th of July, 1995, later in the day. After that, all members of the War Presidency met to discuss the request. In principle, local authorities without an approval of the military and political authorities at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina cannot engage in any local talks, specifically in Zepa in this case. In keeping with that, the War Presidency tried to establish communication by packet communication, which we discussed earlier, in order to discuss this request together with a question to continue or not conveyed to the leadership, specifically in terms of military command. Independently of that, the War Presidency also tried to view all aspects of the situation. The meeting took most of the night between the 12th and the 13th of July. We decided to attend the talks. When we were discussing who was to go, it was decided that I should go with another War Presidency member, Mr. Mujo Omanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just back up and ask a couple of questions to clarify two quick issues. The first is - and this may seem blindingly obvious to you - but can you explain who or which party it was that contacted Colonel Dudnjik originally to get ahold of Colonel Palic? Who reached out to Colonel Dudnjik in the first place?
