utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: The Serb side. I don't know who specifically, though, whether it was the commander of the Rogatica Brigade of the VRS or someone else. I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And you referred to the local authorities, meaning yourself, needing the approval of authorities at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What are you referring to when you speak about authorities at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly what level it is and from what level the answer should have arrived. In any case, we were in contact with Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, the then-president of the Presidency of B&H. At that moment in time we awaited his response, be it an approval or denial. That is in terms of political authorities. As for the military ones, the then-B&H army commander was Rasim Delic. I don't have sufficient information about how the request was conveyed, whether it went through the 2nd Corps or the General Staff. I can't tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you know where President Izetbegovic and Commander Delic were based at this time, sir? Where were they located?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: At this time and generally speaking, President Izetbegovic was in Sarajevo. As for Commander Delic, as far as I know, his main location was in Kakanj with the General Staff. I don't know where they were at that specific point in time, but these were the general locations of both of them, where they usually performed their duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So the decision is made that yourself and Mr. Omanovic will attend. What did you do next?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Mr. Omanovic. Next we informed UNPROFOR, specifically Colonel Dudnjik, who had said earlier that we were to go in an UNPROFOR vehicle and that the meeting was supposed to take place at check-point number 2 of UNPROFOR. The check-point was located at Boksanica, which is on the southern side of the Zepa enclave coming from Rogatica. At that point in time that was the border of the Zepa enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: As far as I recall, although it's been a while, sometime before noon, just before noon, Mujo Omanovic and I got in an UNPROFOR vehicle and went to check-point number 2 at Boksanica. Speaking from memory, I can tell you that on the Serb side we were greeted by General Zdravko Tolimir as well as Lieutenant-Colonel Rajko Kusic, who was the Rogatica Brigade commander of the VRS. To tell you the truth, I didn't know then who General Zdravko Tolimir was because we were under a media blockade and had no electricity; therefore, we couldn't follow any media in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me back up a moment. You described getting in an UNPROFOR vehicle and going to the Boksanica check-point. My first question is: From where did you depart?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: We started in the centre of Zepa from UNPROFOR HQ, which, to repeat, was in the elementary school building in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is your best recollection of what time it was when you set out from the centre of Zepa to go to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: It's difficult to say. Let's say it was between 10.30 and 11.30, that's when we left. I believe it was just before noon or so. That's when we left the centre of Zepa. I do have to say that it was a long time ago and it's difficult to be precise, specifically because I kept no notes at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what's your best estimate as to how long it took you to get to Zepa? And if you can describe just generally again what the terrain is in order to get there.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: I think we should be specific. You probably mean the distance between Zepa and Boksanica?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You're absolutely correct. I misspoke. How long did it take you to get from the centre of Zepa up to Boksanica? Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: I'll give a brief description. Boksanica is south of the Zepa enclave. From the centre of Zepa, one needs to follow a local, narrow road with many bends. To the best of my estimate, given that I had never travelled that route before, in such conditions a ride between the centre of Zepa and check-point number 2 of UNPROFOR at Boksanica took around half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, prior to this meeting you told us that you didn't know who General Tolimir was. Had you ever heard the name of either him or Colonel Kusic prior to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: I said I didn't know who General Tolimir was or what his position was. I may have heard his name on the radio or on TV, but I couldn't say that I remembered much about him. And as for Rajko Kusic, who was either colonel or lieutenant-colonel, I knew who he was. He was the commander of the Rogatica Brigade of the VRS, which effectively manned the lines in front of Zepa. I can also say that I had never met him before, I mean Colonel Rajko Kusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So please tell the Trial Chamber what happened after you met General Tolimir and Colonel Kusic.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, at that meeting the Serbian side was represented by the -- by Zdravko Tolimir, Colonel Kusic. UNPROFOR was represented by Colonel Sejmon Dudnjik, and there was also myself and Mujo Omanovic. At the outset of the meeting, General Tolimir told us something along these lines: Srebrenica has fallen and now it's Zepa's turn. We can go about it in two ways. What I'm offering you is for all of you to leave Zepa, to be evacuated, get on the buses and leave. Then I asked him, "Does this mean that, for example, a 35-year-old man can join his family in getting on the bus and leave to the territory under the control of the BiH Army?" And General Tolimir answered, "Yes, of course." After that, if we decided not to accept that first option, the second option or the alternative was a military solution or, in other words, a military occupation of Zepa. The meeting did not last too long, as far as I can remember. I said to General Tolimir that we were not authorised to make any decisions on the spot there and then. We were only there to listen to the demands or whatever that was that the Serb side had to tell us. We agreed that we would convey the Serbian side demands to the other members of the War Presidency in Zepa and that an answer to the Serb side would be conveyed via UNPROFOR. And in that particular case, I believe that the agreement or the arrangement was for that answer to be conveyed Colonel Sejmon Dudnjik. Speaking from memory, I repeat, the meeting wasn't long and we embarked on the UNPROFOR vehicle again and returned to Zepa. May I continue, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me just follow-up with a couple of questions. What is your best estimate, sir, of how long this meeting lasted?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: It's very hard for me to tell, but I don't think that the meeting lasted any longer than 60 minutes, an hour. But let me repeat, it's very difficult to speak from memory. It was a long time ago, as you know. It may have been a minute or two longer, I suppose, but that is my best recollection and my best estimate of the time that the meeting took.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You described this as a meeting that was not very long. Can you tell the Trial Chamber why it was a meeting that was not very long.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Speaking from memory, according to General Tolimir that was the only item on the agenda, the only topic that had to be discussed, and he said that there was nothing else to talk about. And since we said we were not authorised to discuss any details of a possible evacuation, we left it at that and the meeting ended on that note.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall being asked in the last trial about a document - and this is at transcript page 9852, just for the record - a document that had a time written on it of 10.50 in the morning, ten minutes before 11.00, a document dated the 13th of July? Do you remember noting, and I quote, about the document: "I see this is the 13th of July at 10.50. I think by then we had already left for the -- to attend the negotiations. If the time indicated is correct, as far as I can remember, by then we were already at the negotiations." Do you remember giving that answer, sir, in the Popovic trial?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. And I believe that the document presents the position of the army authorities regarding the legality of our presence at the meeting. I don't know if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's the document I'm speaking about, sir. My question is: You noted, when you saw that document, that the time on the document that it was received in Zepa was --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- ten minutes to 11.00 in the morning. And you testified in the prior trial that: "... as far as I can remember, by then we were already at the negotiations." So my question to you, simply, sir, is: Having heard this excerpt from your prior testimony, can you tell the Trial Chamber which you think is more accurate, that you were already at the negotiations a little before 11.00 on the morning of the 13th or that you departed from the centre of Zepa shortly before noon on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Well, look, I don't know if I have commented upon this before; however, as far as I can remember, we did not wait for any answers as to whether we should go or not. I believe that a decision was locally made for us to go and see what the whole thing was all about. So that this document may have arrived when we were already on the way, but before that decision had been taken to go irrespective of the positions of either the military or political leaders in Sarajevo. That's how I account for this. We did not wait for the document to arrive. The document probably arrived either when we were already on the way or already in the meeting. It's very difficult to tell 15 years after the event. So we were either on the way to Boksanica or already there in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, we have a request. Could we have this portion of the Popovic transcript perhaps on the screen? That would be helpful to understand the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President. And if I could just ask that it not be broadcast because it does have his name at the top. Again, this is from the 2nd of April, 2007, transcript page 9852.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, you are aware that in the today's transcript at the outset we have the name of this current witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that, Mr. President, and we just live with that reality, but thank you for that pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And another question, you put it to the witness in that way that he said, "Just before noon we left Zepa," but in fact I remember that he provided us with two different answers. One was approximately between 10.30 and 11.30, and the other -- the first one was shortly before noon. Just to clarify this -- we have several explanations of the timing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. You're absolutely correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So we -- and that's exactly what I'm getting at. We have an outer limit, shall we say, of a little before noon; we have what the Honourable Presiding Judge just indicated; and now we have your testimony that your recollection was that at the time that this document was received in Zepa at 10.50 in the morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told that there are technical problems because this part of the Popovic transcript is not available in e-court at the moment so that we will lose the Tolimir transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can run it from Sanction, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have now another version on the screen which will not be broadcast. Can you help us and indicate which part of the transcript you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The answer is at lines 8 through 14, and he is being shown an exhibit, as we can see, dated 13th of July, with a time of 10.50 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to welcome everybody present in the courtroom, including the witness. May God's peace reign in the house and may God's will be done. The document hasn't been shown to the witness, he doesn't know what the document is about, and it's up to you to decide whether the document will be shown or not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer was referring to this document. He has it now on the screen in the courtroom so that Mr. Thayer should deal with it with the witness. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I think you've just gotten the transcript page that we've all been talking about on the screen. Do you see the portion that I referred to -- to which I referred in my question, where you say: "... I see this is the 13th of July at 10.50 ..." And then I'll just let you read the rest.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: I need help with the translation of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Could we have the document translated from the screen, if the interpreters have it in front of them on e-court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, in that case -- Mr. Thayer, sorry, I apologise. I think in that case it would be easier if you read this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What line is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Then I will certainly do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We're at line 8 and I'll be reading from line 8 to line 14.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: "I see this document for the first time. Could you please roll it down so that I can see the top of the page? But what I have said stands, there was a lot of confusion. Someone said we could go, someone else that we couldn't. I see this is the 13th of July at 10.50. I think that by then we had already left for the" and there's a pause "-- to attend the negotiations. If the time indicated is correct, as far as I can remember, by then we were already at the negotiations." I think in one of your prior answers, sir, you've already testified that you generally recall what this document was. If you need to see it, I can dig up a copy and we can put it before you, but my question is really focused, I think as you can gather at this time, on the time.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Yes. If possible, I would like to see the document again.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: With the Trial Chamber's permission --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, when you say you want to see the document, you're referring to the actual exhibit and not the trial transcript; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Precisely so. The actual document, not the transcript. That's what I need. I would need to see the document that I saw previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: With the Trial Chamber's permission, we need to do a little freelancing here. This wasn't on our list of exhibits, but it was shown to the witness in the prior trial, as we can all see. I have a copy of the original B/C/S. I can hand it up to the Trial Chamber and then the accused to look at, and then we can place it on the ELMO so we can all see what we're talking about, if that's acceptable to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is, I think, the best way to deal with it, but we would like to know the right number of this document so that we have it on the record precisely. But if we can see it on the ELMO, that's fine. Give it to the Chamber and to Mr. Tolimir and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. For the record, it is in the Popovic case Defence Exhibit 5D275, and we'll see the ERN in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, do you have a number of your 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. This was a Defence exhibit that was used and was not put on our 65 ter list. It was, as I said, obviously shown to him by the Defence during the Popovic trial, but it's not something that we included on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, would you agree with this procedure? Mr. Tolimir, I would like to ask you again if you agree with this procedure proposed by Mr. Thayer, to put it on the ELMO so that everybody can see it on the ELMO and it could be read out and then be part of the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that I have a solution. I don't know whether the documents the Defence is going to be using have been loaded up in e-court, but let's try with the document 65 ter 1D247. That's a Defence document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm being told, Mr. President, it's not uploaded yet, though I thank Mr. Gajic for the effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take I didn't understand correctly what you were proposing, Mr. Gajic. The question stands if Mr. Tolimir is in agreement with the procedure Mr. Thayer was going to use?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. There's no problem there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In this case, Mr. Thayer, no objection by the Defence. We can see this document on the ELMO and the witness should perhaps read out the relevant portion so that we have it on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, if you would take a moment. Fortunately it's a relatively short document. And if you could read into the record the document starting from the heading on the far left, where it says "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Very well. Can I start?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The text of the document reads -- may I continue, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Heading: "The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. "The army General Staff." In the right-hand side corner: "Republican defence, military secret, strictly confidential number 1 [as interpreted], date 13 July 1995." I have to go back to the number, 1/825-1135. "Date: 13 July 1995. "Op.vr," probably stands for operational time, "10.50 hours. "Response to request to be sent to. "The command of the 285th Light Mountain Brigade Zepa (to be forwarded to the president of the War Presidency of Zepa). "With regard to the message sent to the president of the government of the republic R/F BiH by the president of the War Presidency of Zepa, we have received the following answer from the Presidency: "We inform the president of the War Presidency of Zepa that there should be no negotiations with the aggressor. "What you can expect from the aggressor is an unconditional ultimatum for surrender. "The people and combatants of Zepa must continue their preparations for an organised resistance to the aggressor and prevent an onset of panic, and they have to take a decisive action to convince the population about the possibility of a successful resistance against the aggressor. "The Presidency and the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina have invested maximum effort on international, military, and political levels. "Regards." Signed by the Chief of Staff, General Enver Hadzihasanovic. And that's the entire text of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Witness. Now, having read that document back --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we can have that transcript page back up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In your answer in the last trial you testified, and this is at line 11: "I see this is the 13th of July at 10.50." And as you just read out, the operational time was 10.50 on the document. "I think that by then we had already left for the -- to attend the negotiations. If the time indicated is correct, as far as I can remember, by then we were already at the negotiations." So back to the question. You've testified today that you recall a time of shortly before noon. You also recall that you think you left from the centre of Zepa sometime between 10.30 and 11.30. And we see here that your recollection when you saw this document in 2007 --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- was that by ten minutes to 11.00 you were already at the negotiations. So the question just simply is: Can you provide the Trial Chamber with any clear recollection of when it was that you think, let's say, you arrived at Boksanica?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: In my view, judging on the -- by the time I believe we left, the arrival could have taken place between 11.00 and 12.00, the arrival at Boksanica, that is. As for the time shown on the document, in my previous testimony I said that, as far as I recall, we left to attend the negotiations regardless of the opinion of our political authorities, and we see here that it was a negative one. This is what I can remember, and I hope you understand that it's been 15 years, which is a long time for someone to try and put things in the right order and exact time. So perhaps the answer to your question is that if we had left between 10.30 and 11.30 and if it had taken 30 minutes to travel, we would have been at Boksanica in relation to the estimated starting time between 11.00 and 12.00 on the 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And we certainly don't take it for granted the taxation we're placing on your recollection here. And before we break for the night, just one other effort to test your memory a little bit. You testified that you believed that the meeting was short, that it might have lasted an hour or a minute or two more. Do you recall in the Popovic trial - and this is at page 9725 - saying that you think it lasted between 40 minutes and an hour? Do you recall that testimony; and if so, does that affect your testimony today at all?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: It does not. I can generally remember without referring to any notes that it took around that time. What I have said, that it was probably between 40 minutes and one hour, is basically what I can recall about that meeting, its duration, and our arrival and departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, back to the meeting, sir. Just for one last question about the meeting itself. You testified - and I think you used the words when you were just characterising what General Tolimir told you - you said when he gave you the choice of -- between the two options, he said "all of you." When he said "all of you," what did he mean?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK
utterances.text: Well, the whole population of Zepa, including the military-aged men. In any case, "all of you" meant the entire population of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if -- with the Court's permission, I'm about to go to the next chapter and I sense that the -- this might be a good time to call it a day a couple minutes early if that's all right. And I do actually have a proposal that I can make to the Trial Chamber in the absence of the witness, if the Court permits, concerning the witness that the Trial Chamber issued its decision on earlier today that we have available to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before we do that, we have questions for the witness. I would like to ask one question, sir. We were looking at document, the response from your authorities of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina to your request how to deal with this request to meet for negotiations. Did you receive this response before you left Zepa for this check-point 1 and for the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I said that, that as far as I recall, I do not remember having received it before our departure to attend negotiations. However, independently of that, we locally decided to attend them. Even if we had received it by that time, I don't think it would have changed anything; we would still have left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But you decided to attend this meeting with Mr. Tolimir and the other lieutenant-colonel without having received a response from your superiors, from the higher authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, it was precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge Nyambe has a further question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I think I may have three clarifications. The first one, immediately here you have said -- you have said something to the effect that General Tolimir said you were to leave the area of Zepa and that in a question from -- I want to get it exactly. Yeah. It is page 63, lines 10. "... between the two options he said 'all of you.' When he said 'all of you' what did he mean?" And your answer has been: "The whole population of Zepa, including military-aged men." My question is a clarification. Was the entire population of Zepa Muslim or mixed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The entire population of Zepa save for a single lady was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I have another question. This comes -- okay. Yeah. I have another question. This comes on page 38 of today's transcript, lines 14 to 16. In answer to the question from the Prosecution you state: "According to my estimate, about 1200 able-bodied men." In Zepa, were present in Zepa at that particular point. You go on to say: "Let me just say they were not all combatants ..." Are you able to give an estimation approximately how many were combatants and how many were not combatants? That's the first question. The second one: How were you able to tell who was a combatant and who was not a combatant? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to your first question, the estimation of how many combatants there were -- well, I think there were some 600 of them who were directly participating in the work of the brigade. As for who was and was not a combatant, well, that mainly has to do with their engagement in the previous period in the army. Those who had weapons were considered combatants, if I can use that term. Those who did not and yet fell within that age category, between 18 and, say, 55 years of age, that was the rest of that group, in my view, it was 600 of them as well. So one group had 600 and the other had 600. Of course, I have to note that it is mainly based on my estimation and is not founded on any exact lists or documents. I don't have any and I don't remember ever having seen such documents in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Just another follow-up question. Your estimation is based on documents or on observation of the group that was in Zepa at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My estimate is based on the knowledge I had while I was in Zepa. What does that mean? Perhaps I can try and explain. I may have heard from, say, Avdo, the commander or one of his associates that approximately 600 men had weapons. I base my estimate on that, not on any documents. I did not see any lists of those who were or were not there. I believe I stressed already that what I'm telling you was based on the information I had that was gained either by speaking to someone who was in the know or by what I could observe. Zepa is a small location. It all took place in a geographically small circle. The centre of Zepa is perhaps 50 metres in diameter, and this is how I learned things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Presiding Judge. I wanted to say the following, that there was a misinterpretation of my words by the witness. I told him that I -- that anybody could leave Zepa. He asked me: Does that mean a soldier with his family? And I responded positively. It is in lines 8 to 11. I just wanted to reflect accurately what I said and what the witness responded without any misinterpretations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We heard that, Mr. Tolimir, but in fact you are not giving evidence. You are -- we have a different position, we in the Trial Chamber, and you may deal with it in the cross-examination. Mr. Thayer, we are really over time now, but what about the documents we have recently seen? Are you tendering any of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had not intended to show or anticipated showing that to the witness, but I think it would be a good -- well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You may consider this question --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- and you have time to come back to that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Excellent suggestion, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness, for today we are at the end of your examination. It will continue tomorrow in the afternoon. I would like to remind you that you are not allowed to get in contact to either party about the content of your testimony. The Court Officer will assist you while leaving the courtroom. The windows should be -- screens should be brought down so that Mr. Thayer is able to address something, procedure matters to the Court. Thank you and we continue tomorrow. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect to the witness number 205, PW-076, about who the Trial Chamber issued its oral decision earlier today, I think as we notified the parties, that witness is here and he is available. He will be, I think, a relatively brief witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What I have proposed to the Defence and which the Defence has accepted, so that that witness isn't sitting here during the entirety of the current witness's testimony, which I think will be extensive, I think it will take us through the last sitting of this week and possibly more, would be to interrupt this witness's testimony briefly to lead that witness's testimony, cross-examine, and then be able to send him home. He does face some employment repercussions the longer he is here, and we would propose that we just call a brief timeout from this witness and be able to put that witness on and then resume with the current witness shortly thereafter. And he is available any time should the Court desire to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, what is your positio? Or Mr. Gajic? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I spoke with Mr. Thayer before this sitting, and we agreed that that witness should start his testimony tomorrow morning and that he would probably be concluded tomorrow, whereupon Mr. Thayer would resume his examination-in-chief of the current witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber appreciates this proposal so that the witness has not to stay too long in The Hague. But, Mr. Gajic, we can't resume with this witness tomorrow morning but only in the afternoon. We are sitting in the afternoon. So that we are really over time now but at the end of today's hearing we will first have the witness PW-076, if I'm not mistaken, and then we'll resume tomorrow in the afternoon in this courtroom. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 24th day of August, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25
